content: The document titled Guidelines for the Care and Treatment of Persons Diagnosed with Chronic Hepatitis C Virus Infection was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in July 2018. It provides evidence-based recommendations for the management of chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. 1. Background: In 2015, an estimated 71 million people worldwide were living with chronic HCV infection, and 399,000 deaths were attributed to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma caused by HCV. In 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) on viral hepatitis, aiming to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. This includes a 90% reduction in new infections and a 65% reduction in mortality. 7. Rationale for Updates: Since the last update in 2016, three key developments have influenced the guidelines: The availability of safe and highly effective direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens for all individuals with chronic HCV infection, supporting a strategy of treating all infected persons rather than reserving treatment for those with advanced disease. The approval of several new pangenotypic DAA medicines, reducing the need for genotyping to guide treatment decisions. Substantial reductions in the cost of DAAs, enabling rapid treatment rollout in many lowand middle-income countries. 8. Scope of the Guidelines: The guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for the care and treatment of individuals diagnosed with chronic HCV infection. This includes addressing when to initiate treatment, which treatments to use, and how to monitor and manage patients effectively. 9. Glossary of Terms: Acute HCV Infection: A new HCV infection that may or may not present with symptoms. Chronic HCV Infection: Persistent HCV infection lasting six months or more. Cirrhosis: Extensive liver scarring due to prolonged inflammation, classified as compensated (without symptoms) or decompensated (with complications such as ascites or variceal bleeding). Sustained Virological Response (SVR12): The absence of detectable HCV RNA in the blood 12 weeks after completing treatment, considered equivalent to a cure. Pangenotypic: Antiviral medicines effective against all major HCV genotypes. 10. Key Recommendations: The guidelines emphasize the importance of diagnosing 90% of those infected and treating 80% of diagnosed individuals to achieve the elimination targets set by the GHSS. They also highlight the need for continued research, cost-effectiveness analysis, and the development of data systems to monitor care quality and outcomes. This document serves as a comprehensive resource for healthcare professionals involved in the management of chronic HCV infection, providing detailed guidance on evidence-based practices and strategies for achieving global elimination goals.
